lesson.title: Le Manteau & La Robe
lesson.subtitle: Clothing doublets (manteau/mantle, robe/wardrobe) and adjective placement with colors.

hook.title: Wardrobe Doublets & Wearing Clothes: Le Manteau & La Robe
hook.content: Old French mantel ('cloak/coat') gave English 'mantle' and softened into modern French le manteau (just like castel → château and gastel → gâteau!). Frankish *rauba gave French la robe ('dress') and English 'wardrobe'. And to say 'I am wearing', French uses porter ('to carry/wear'): Je porte un manteau noir!

footnotes.title: Look at the -el → -eau sound law: castle/château, gateau, mantle/manteau!
footnotes.content: Old French -el vocalized into modern French -eau (/o/): castel → château, mantel → manteau, bel → beau, nouvel → nouveau!

pattern.title: porter ('to wear / carry') + Noun + Color in Back (and BAGS in Front)
pattern.content: Combine clothing nouns with BAGS adjectives in front and color adjectives in back.
pattern.linguist_note: Old French dark /ɫ/ vocalization to -eau (/o/) explains English -el/-le vs. French -eau doublets.
pattern.trap_note: Remember: color adjectives agree with the clothing noun and stand AFTER it: un manteau blanc (m.) vs. une robe blanche (f.)!

exercises.prompt: Match each French -eau word with its English -el/-le doublet and meaning:
exercises.target_answer: the coat / overcoat (mantle), the castle, the cake, beautiful / handsome, new (novel)
exercises.meaning: le manteau (Old French mantel), le château (Old French castel), le gâteau (Old French gastel), beau / bel (Old French bel), nouveau / nouvel (Old French nouvel)
exercises.explanation: Old French -el turned into modern French -eau (/o/) across nouns and adjectives alike!

exercises.prompt: French le manteau ('the coat') is the -el → -eau twin of which English word for a cloak (or the shelf above a fireplace)?
exercises.explanation: Old French mantel became English mantle and modern French manteau.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'a beautiful white dress' (la robe is feminine)?
exercises.explanation: belle (BAGS) steps in front of robe, and blanche (Color, feminine of blanc) stands after robe!

exercises.idea: I am wearing a black coat today (use Je porte un manteau noir)
cues: a black coat today → un manteau noir aujourd'hui
idea_parts: object + color + time → un manteau noir aujourd'hui
exercises.target_answer: Je porte un manteau noir aujourd'hui
exercises.meaning: I am wearing a black coat today
exercises.explanation: manteau is masculine, so noir stays masculine after it.

diagnosis.cue: Place masculine noir after manteau: un manteau noir.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Elle a acheté une jolie robe rouge
exercises.target_answer: Elle a acheté une jolie robe rouge
exercises.meaning: She bought a pretty red dress
exercises.explanation: jolie (BAGS) in front of robe, rouge (color) in back.
exercises.affirmation: You flanked robe with jolie and rouge cleanly!

summary.outcome: Decode the -el → -eau doublet law (manteau/mantle, château/castle, beau/bel) and describe clothing with porter, BAGS, and colors.

use_example.german: Il fait froid, donc je porte mon grand manteau bleu.
use_example.english: It's cold, so I'm wearing my big blue coat.

summary.takeaway: Old French -el became modern French -eau (mantle → manteau, castle → château).
summary.curiosity_teaser: You have completed every core, sprig, and support branch on Le Pont — félicitations !

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "I am wearing a black coat today" in French:
twist.target_answer: Je porte un manteau noir aujourd'hui
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Je porte un manteau noir aujourd'hui" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Le Manteau & La Robe.

manteau.etymology_derivation: Old French mantel → manteau; English kept 'mantle'.

robe.etymology_derivation: In everyday French, une robe is any woman's dress.

bleu.shift_rule: Frankish blao — one Germanic word, two languages
bleu.etymology_derivation: Frankish *blao gave English blue and French bleu — a Germanic word inside Romance, no shift needed.

rouge.etymology_derivation: Latin rubeus 'red' — the same stone English calls ruby. Rouge crossed into English as the makeup word.

noir.etymology_derivation: Placed after the noun, like all color adjectives.

blanc.etymology_derivation: Germanic blank 'shining white' → French blanc, English blank and blanket (the white cloth).

vert.etymology_derivation: Latin viridis → verdant, verdure — the green English kept in poetry.

beau.etymology_derivation: BAGS adjective: steps before the noun! Becomes bel before a vowel (un bel hôtel) and belle in the feminine.

nouveau.etymology_derivation: Steps before the noun; nouvel before a vowel, nouvelle in the feminine.
